title: CMEA and the Demand for NIEO

cards.h: Two challenges to the Western economic order
cards.b:
The Bretton Woods order was built by the West. Two groups tried other paths. The Soviet bloc set up its own trading system, the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (CMEA or COMECON). The newly independent states of the Global South demanded a New International Economic Order (NIEO).

Both failed in their own ways. The CMEA collapsed with communism in 1991. The NIEO was blocked by rich states and undercut by the 1980s debt crisis. Yet the questions they raised, about fair prices, technology, debt and voice in global bodies, are alive today in BRICS, G20 and climate-finance debates.

UPSC asks you to explain each, compare them with Bretton Woods, and judge why the NIEO failed. India, a leader of the G-77 and NAM, is central to the NIEO story.

The CMEA was founded in Moscow in January 1949 by the USSR, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland and Romania. It was Stalin's answer to the Marshall Plan (1947), which Moscow had forbidden its satellites to accept.

  • Albania joined in 1949 but stopped taking part in 1961.
  • East Germany joined in 1950.
  • Non-European members came later: Mongolia (1962), Cuba (1972) and Vietnam (1978).
  • Yugoslavia had an associate status from 1964.

Headquarters: Moscow. Its stated aim was planned economic cooperation and a "socialist division of labour" among members. In practice it linked Eastern European economies to the Soviet Union.

• Bilateral barter-like trade. Trade was agreed in five-year plans between governments, not through markets.
  • Prices were set by formulas, often based on past world-market prices.
  • Transferable rouble. A unit of account cleared through the International Bank for Economic Cooperation (1963). It was not freely convertible.
  • Energy for goods. The USSR supplied oil and gas, often below world prices after 1973, in exchange for machinery and consumer goods. The Druzhba ("Friendship") pipeline (1960s) is a symbol.
  • Comprehensive Programme (1971) aimed at deeper integration and joint investment.

Specialisation dispute

In 1962 Khrushchev proposed a supranational planning body that would assign roles to each country. Romania objected, fearing it would be kept as a farm supplier, and the plan was shelved. National sovereignty limited integration, unlike the EEC.

• No price signals. Without markets, prices did not show real costs. Waste and shortages followed.
  • Low quality and technology. Members traded goods that could not compete in the West.
  • Soviet dominance. Members resented the hub-and-spoke structure. The USSR's subsidies were also a political tool.
  • Inconvertible currencies blocked multilateral trade.
  • Debt. Poland and Hungary borrowed heavily from the West in the 1970s.
  • Politics. The 1989 revolutions removed the regimes that made it work.

In 1991 members moved to world prices and hard currency. The CMEA was formally dissolved in June 1991, months before the USSR itself.

Compare with the EEC: market-based, rule-bound and supranational, it deepened while the CMEA dissolved. Many former CMEA states later joined the EU (2004, 2007).

Newly independent states found that political freedom did not bring economic freedom. They still exported raw materials and imported manufactures on unfavourable terms (the Prebisch-Singer thesis).

  • 1962. UN resolution 1803 on permanent sovereignty over natural resources.
  • 1964. The first UNCTAD in Geneva, led by Raul Prebisch. The G-77 formed on 15 June 1964.
  • 1968. UNCTAD II in New Delhi pushed the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP).
  • 1970. UN target that rich states give 0.7% of GNP as aid.
  • 1973. NAM's Algiers summit called for a new order. That October, the OPEC oil embargo and price rise showed commodity power.

Encouraged by OPEC, the South pressed its case at the UN.

The UN General Assembly's Sixth Special Session adopted on 1 May 1974 the Declaration on the Establishment of a New International Economic Order (resolution 3201) and a Programme of Action (3202). In December 1974 the Assembly adopted the Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States (resolution 3281), over Western objections.

Main demands

  • Stable, fair commodity prices, and indexation to the prices of manufactures.
  • The right to regulate and nationalise foreign firms.
  • Technology transfer on fair terms; a code of conduct for multinationals.
  • Preferential, non-reciprocal access to rich markets.
  • More aid and debt relief.
  • Reform of the IMF and World Bank to give the South a bigger voice.
  • Producer associations, like OPEC, for other commodities.

• UNCTAD IV (Nairobi, 1976) adopted an Integrated Programme for Commodities and a Common Fund, agreed in 1980 but only in force in 1989, far smaller than planned.
  • The EEC's Lome Convention (1975) with African, Caribbean and Pacific states gave trade preferences and STABEX export-earnings support.
  • The Brandt Report, North-South: A Programme for Survival (1980), urged mutual interest and large transfers.
  • The Cancun summit (1981), with Reagan and Indira Gandhi, produced little.

• Northern resistance. The US, UK and West Germany rejected price controls and nationalisation rules. Reagan and Thatcher (from 1979-81) championed free markets.
  • The debt crisis (from Mexico, 1982) shifted power to creditors. The IMF's structural adjustment replaced the NIEO agenda.
  • Divided South. Oil price rises hurt oil-importing developing countries. East Asian states chose export-led growth.
  • Commodity cartels failed beyond oil. Producers of copper, coffee or bauxite could not hold prices.
  • UN votes are not binding. General Assembly resolutions lacked enforcement.
  • Neoliberal turn in ideas: the Washington Consensus (1989).

Some analysts (Robert Rothstein, Stephen Krasner's Structural Conflict, 1985) argued the South sought authority-based regimes because it lacked market power.

The NIEO is often called dead, but its themes returned.

  • Voice. G20 (leaders from 2008), IMF quota reform, the African Union in the G20 (2023).
  • Alternatives. BRICS and its New Development Bank, the AIIB.
  • Climate justice. CBDR, loss and damage, and the $300 billion finance goal (2024) echo the call for transfers.
  • Debt. The G20 Common Framework (2020), and calls for a UN debt mechanism.
  • Technology. The COVID-19 TRIPS waiver fight (2020-22).
  • Sovereignty over resources. Critical minerals policies in Indonesia and Africa.

Scholars such as Vijay Prashad (The Darker Nations, 2007) see the NIEO as the high point of a Third World project. Others see the shift to market reform as a better route.

• Rupee trade with the Soviet bloc. India was not a CMEA member, but it traded with the USSR and Eastern Europe through rupee-rouble clearing agreements (from 1953), paying in goods rather than hard currency. Soviet help built Bhilai (steel) and other plants.
  • After 1991. Russia and India settled the old rouble debt in 1993. Rupee trade ideas resurfaced after the 2022 sanctions on Russia, when the RBI allowed trade settlement in rupees (July 2022).
  • NIEO leadership. India hosted UNCTAD II (New Delhi, 1968), was a founding G-77 member, and chaired NAM from 1983. Indira Gandhi championed the NIEO, and attended the 1981 Cancun summit.
  • Today. India speaks for the Global South: Voice of Global South summits (2023 onwards), debt and climate finance, and WTO food security. It chaired BRICS in 2026.

"Why did the demand for a New International Economic Order fail? Is it relevant today?"
"Examine the role and failure of COMECON."
"Compare the CMEA with the European Economic Community."

Structure for CMEA: origin (1949, reply to Marshall Plan), members, working (plans, transferable rouble, Soviet energy), Romania's 1962 dispute, failure and dissolution (June 1991), comparison with EEC.

Structure for NIEO: roots (Prebisch, UNCTAD 1964, G-77, OPEC 1973), 1974 Declaration and Charter, demands, outcomes (Common Fund, Lome, Brandt), reasons for failure, legacy today, India's role.
